some of the co co-sharers, sharers, namely Gurcharan Singh etc. whose land was acquired along with that of Bachan Singh filed a suit for possession.

Plaintiffs accordi accordingly ngly sought possession back of the acquired land.

[9] Acquisition of the land for the purpose of installation of brick- brick klin for the construction of Bhakra canal is not disputed.
Defendants however claimed that entire entire compensation was paid to the original owners.

As per the defendants, plaintiffs have no right right, title or interest vested in them to get the possession of the acquired land back from the defendants.

sentences.text: At this juncture, it would be relevant to refer to certain instructions and paragraphs of the said Administration Manual on which reliance has been placed by the plaintiffs.

The relevant paragraphs in the administration manual are as follows:
follows:-
"493: Disposal of land no longer required.

Where the land in the permanent occupation of any department of the Punjab Govt. is no longer required it should he handed over to the Deputy Commissioner of the District, who becomes responsible for the disposal of it under the orders of the Commissioner.
It may not, however, be permanently alienated without the previous sanction legal he Government.
There is no legal bar on it being put into auction.

But ass a matter of grace, Government is usually willing to restore agricultural and pastoral land to the persons from whom it acquired it or to their heirs on their refunding the amount paid as compensation lean the 15% granted for compulsory acquisition.

The pprice rice may be lowered, if necessary on account of deterioration, or 4 of 13 RSA-5005-2013 2013 (O&M) enhanced in the rare case of land having been Improved by the use to which the Government had put it.
The improvement must be one affecting the quality of the land.
The fact that the land wh which ich was unirrigated at the time of acquisition, can when relinquished, be watered by a canal is not an improvement of this sort.
Considering how great the rise in the market value of the land has been the terms stated above are very liberal.

It is not nece necessary ssary to adopt them in their entirety where the persons concerned are remote descendants or relations of the original holders and where the circumstances of the case are at all out of the common.

When for example, no price, or merely a nominal price was paid id to the owner in the First Instance, or when the rise in the value of land in the neighborhood has been exceptionally large, these facts should he pointed out when referring such cases for orders.
That the Govt. may have sufficient material before it to decide whether to offer any special terms to the heirs of the persons from whom that land was acquired."
"494: Case in which preference should be given to owners of adjoining fields.

In the case of plots from which from their size or shape are practically of no value to anyone but the owners of the adjoining fields, the government will be prepared to consider proposals for giving these owners the option of purchasing at the market value.

The mere fact that an outsider is prepared to outbid them should not deter the Deputy Commissioner from recommending to Government the acceptance of any fair offer which they may make."
495. Action when the heirs and neighboring proprietors do not wish to purchase.

If the heirs of the original owners cannot be traced, or if they or the proprietors of adjoining lands decline to accept the terms approved by the Government, a further referral to Government will be necessary if it is proposed to alienate the land permanently In some other way."

sentences.text: 5 ) The Financial Commissioner has also Standing Orders.

Paragraph 87 of the Financial Commissioner Standing Order No.28 is as follows:
"When agricultural or pastoral land is permanently acquired for public purposes by any department of the Govt. and is no longer required for such purposes, urposes, the disposal of it shall be guided by the general considerations mentioned in paragraphs 493 to 495 of the Land Administration Manual which are reproduced below.
6.

Briefly stated, therefore, the admitted position is that the lands which were acquired quired for a public purpose, when not required any more for that public purpose, just like a case in this matter, is expected to be disposed of in terms of above referred policy adopted by the Government.
Nothing was placed before me on behalf of the State to indicate that the plaintiffs would be otherwise not entitled to return of the land.
It, therefore, clearly follows that in terms of the policy referred to above, the plaintiffs would be entitled to return of the land in question.
In my opinion, the Additional itional District Judge committed error in non non-suiting suiting the plaintiffs on the ground that the plaintiffs cannot claim the land as a matter of right.

It may be stated that the total reading of the paragraphs 493 to 495, referred above,
and the Standing Order 28, would indicate that the Government has adopted as a matter of policy to return the land to the original owner under the circumstances covered by those paragraphs.
There seems no good reason, therefore, to deprive the plaintiffs from getting the benefit of that policy.

If the plaintiffs are unjustifiably deprived of the policy thus adopted by the Government and followed In respect of other similarly situated cases, the plaintiffs can come to the Court to seek direction from the court for enforcement of tthe he said policy.
There is no good reason to discriminate the plaintiffs and deprive them of the benefits under the said policy.
7. The appellate Court also committed error in thinking that in respect of the grievance regarding discrimination, the remedy ooff the plaintiffs was by way of writ petition.
May be that writ petition would be one of the modes to enforce the policy and seek redress from the Court.
But, if the plaintiffs filed civil suit to obtain some relief, they cannot be denied that relief simply because such a relief could have been available by way of writ petition also.

It is not only a question for discrimination against the plaintiffs, but is also called upon the State, to show why the 6 of 13 RSA-5005-2013 2013 (O&M) policy adopted by it cannot be made applicable in case of the plaintiffs.
The Government by forming the policy, as stated above, has almost given an understanding to the person's that they would be entitled to get back the land under certain conditions and circumstances.
Since the plaintiffs fulfill those conditions ions and circumstances, they are entitled to get the land in terms of the paragraphs and the Standing Orders referred above.
In view of that, I allow the appeal."

Shri Naik, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners, contended that in the second writ petition, the petitioner sought restitution of the possession pursuant to the t resolution of the State Government dated 10.10.1973 under which the Government directed that the surplus land was to be utilised first for any other public purpose and in the alternative it was to be given back to the erstwhile owners.

sentences.text: [18] Considering the aforesaid precedents, this Court finds that the issue would be covered in favour of the appellants in view of ratio of law laid down by Supreme Court in 'Gurcharan Singh's case (ibid).

Division Bench in Dalip Singh and others's case (supra) and in 'Dr. Vijay Khosla another case (supra) rightly held that Standing Order and another's rder 28 and paragraph 493 of the Land Administration Manual do not create any right in favour of any person to get back possession of the acquired land.
The said proposition finds approval from Supreme Court in Gurcharan Singh's case (supra) as well.
However, issue involved is beyond that.
The question is 'whether a Government having taken up a Policy Decision can implement the same selectively without any reasonable classification?

[19] Answer is 'No'' and so has been held by the Supreme Court.
Once it has come on record that Government acted upon a Policy Decision ecision 12 of 13 RSA-5005-2013 2013 (O&M) and released land in favour of similarly situated persons, there is no reason that the plaintiffs in the present case be denied the same relief.
Denying the relief to the present appellants would be denying them right to equality enshrined in the Constitution tion of India as a fundamental right.

[20] In view of the above, this Court finds that the judgment and decree passed by the Courts below cannot be sustained being in teeth of ratio of law laid down by the Supreme Court in ''Gurcharan Singh's case (ibid).
(ibid)
[21] Accordingly, the present appeal preferred by the plaintiffs is allowed.
They are held entitled to get the possession of the land back in terms of the law laid down by the Supreme Court.
The objection raised by the defendants regarding non-impleadment non impleadment of Department of Forest cannot sustain and sans merit.
Once, State of Harya Haryana itself is a party in the suit, there was no need for the plaintiffs to implead the Departments.
[22] Suit filed by the plaintiffs succeeds.
Decree be drawn.
[23] All pending miscellaneous application(s), if any, stands disposed off.
